exercises.prompt:
What does this print? Write it with single spaces.

```r
x <- c(3, 10, 10, 14, 20, 29)
hist(x, breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 10), plot = FALSE)$counts
```

feedback.message: Not yet. That counts each bin as including its left edge. R's `hist()` includes the right edge: the bins are (0,10], (10,20] and (20,30].

hints: The breaks make three bins: 0 to 10, 10 to 20 and 20 to 30.
A value exactly on a break, such as 10, belongs to the bin that ends there.
exercises.solution: By default `hist()` uses right-closed bins, (0,10], (10,20] and (20,30], so a value on a break belongs to the bin on its left. The first bin holds 3, 10 and 10; the second 14 and 20; the third 29. R prints `[1] 3 2 1`. Pass `right = FALSE` for left-closed bins, and always check which convention a table of bands uses when you report it.

exercises.prompt:
A box plot draws points beyond the whiskers individually. How many values does this print?

```r
boxplot.stats(c(10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 2, 30))$out
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Outliers can be unusually small as well as unusually large: look at the 2 as well as the 30.
Not yet. The box runs from 11 to 15.5, so anything more than 1.5 × 4.5 = 6.75 beyond it is drawn separately.

hints: The box spans the lower and upper hinges, here 11 and 15.5.
Points more than 1.5 box-lengths beyond the box are outliers, at either end.
exercises.solution: The five numbers are 10, 11, 13.5, 15.5 and 16: the box runs from 11 to 15.5, a length of 4.5. Anything below 11 − 6.75 = 4.25 or above 15.5 + 6.75 = 22.25 is drawn on its own, so `$out` holds **2** values, `[1]  2 30`. The whiskers stop at the most extreme values still inside those limits, 10 and 16.

exercises.prompt: A colleague's analysis script begins with `install.packages("ggplot2")` followed by `library(ggplot2)`. What is the best change?

options.label: Remove `install.packages()` from the script, keep `library(ggplot2)`, and record the dependency, for example with renv.
options.feedback: Yes. Installing is a one-time change to a machine; attaching is what every run needs.

options.label: Remove `library(ggplot2)`, because installing a package also attaches it.
options.feedback: Not yet. Installing puts the package on disk; only `library()` (or `pkg::fun`) makes its functions available in a session.

options.label: Nothing: reinstalling on every run guarantees the newest version.
options.feedback: Not yet. It needs a network, slows every run, changes the user's machine, and the newest version may change your results.

options.label: Replace both lines with `source("ggplot2")`.
options.feedback: Not yet. `source()` runs an R script file; it does not install or attach packages.

hints: Which of the two lines needs to run every time, and which only once per machine?
exercises.solution: `install.packages()` downloads and installs, once per machine or renv project; `library()` attaches an installed package in every session. A script should only attach. Record what it depends on in `renv.lock` (or at least a README), so that `renv::restore()` can install exactly the right versions.

exercises.prompt: The stats package, attached by default, has a function `filter()`. You then run `library(dplyr)`, which also defines `filter()`. Which function does a plain call `filter(...)` now use?

options.label: dplyr's, because the package attached last comes first in `search()`; write `stats::filter()` to reach the other.
options.feedback: Yes. R looks through the search path in order, and `library()` puts the new package near the front.

options.label: stats's, because base and recommended packages always take priority.
options.feedback: Not yet. Attaching dplyr puts it ahead of stats in the search path, which is why R prints a "masked" message.

options.label: Neither: R stops with an error about an ambiguous name.
options.feedback: Not yet. R allows the clash and resolves it by search order, printing a message when the package is attached.

options.label: Whichever matches the arguments better.
options.feedback: Not yet. R does not choose between plain functions by their arguments; it takes the first one it finds on the search path.

hints: Recall what `search()` lists, and where `library()` adds a package.
exercises.solution: R finds names by walking the search path from the front: your workspace, then the most recently attached package, and so on down to base. After `library(dplyr)`, dplyr's `filter` masks the one in stats. Writing `dplyr::filter()` or `stats::filter()` removes all doubt, which is why many professionals use the `pkg::fun` form in scripts.

exercises.prompt: You used renv in a project. Which file must you commit to Git so that a colleague can install exactly the package versions you used?

options.label: `renv.lock`
options.feedback: Yes. It records every package with its exact version and source, and `renv::restore()` installs from it.

options.label: The whole `renv/library/` folder of installed packages
options.feedback: Not yet. The installed packages are large and specific to one operating system and R version; renv rebuilds them from the lockfile.

options.label: `.RData`
options.feedback: Not yet. That is a saved workspace of objects, which records nothing about package versions and is best not used at all.

options.label: The output of `search()` pasted into the README
options.feedback: Not yet. `search()` lists attached packages without versions or sources.

exercises.solution: **`renv.lock`.** `renv::snapshot()` writes it, `renv::restore()` reads it, and it is small text that belongs in version control next to the code. The project library itself is ignored by Git and rebuilt on each machine.

exercises.prompt: In the lesson's ToothGrowth plot, what do you change to draw violin plots instead of box plots, keeping everything else the same?

options.label: Replace `geom_boxplot()` with `geom_violin()`.
options.feedback: Yes. The geom decides how the data is drawn; the data, mappings, facets, labels and theme stay as they are.

options.label: Change `aes(x = factor(dose), y = len, fill = supp)` to `aes(violin = len)`.
options.feedback: Not yet. Aesthetics map columns to visual properties such as position and colour; the kind of shape drawn is the geom's job.

options.label: Replace `theme_minimal()` with `theme_violin()`.
options.feedback: Not yet. Themes control non-data elements such as backgrounds and fonts, and there is no `theme_violin()`.

options.label: Rewrite the plot with base graphics, since ggplot2 cannot draw violins.
options.feedback: Not yet. ggplot2 has `geom_violin()`; swapping a geom is exactly what the grammar makes easy.

hints: Which part of the grammar of graphics is the geometric object that represents the data?
exercises.solution: Swap the **geom**: `geom_violin()` in place of `geom_boxplot()`. Because ggplot2 separates data, aesthetic mappings, geoms, facets and themes, changing one part leaves the others untouched.

exercises.prompt: What does `all.equal(1, 1.1)` print? Write it exactly as R prints it, with single spaces.

feedback.message: Not yet. When the values differ, `all.equal()` does not return `FALSE`: it returns a description of the difference. That is why tests wrap it in `isTRUE()`.

hints: `all.equal()` returns `TRUE` when the values agree within a tolerance. What does it return otherwise?
exercises.solution: It prints `[1] "Mean relative difference: 0.1"`: a character string describing how far apart the values are, not `FALSE`. So `if (all.equal(a, b))` fails with an error when they differ, and the lesson's `expect_equal()` uses `isTRUE(all.equal(actual, expected))`, which is `TRUE` or `FALSE` in every case.
